questions.scenario: A human resources team wants an agent in Microsoft Foundry that answers employee questions by using the content of three policy documents that the team uploads.
questions.question: Which tool should you add to the agent?

options.why: Correct. File search indexes uploaded files so that the agent can answer from their content.
Code interpreter runs Python for calculations and file processing. It does not ground answers in policy text.
Web search returns public web results. Internal policy documents are not on the public web.
Function calling asks the client app to run a function that you define. It is not needed to search uploaded documents.

questions.explanation: File search is the knowledge tool that lets an agent retrieve and cite content from documents that you upload.

questions.question: Which TWO components must you specify when you create a prompt agent in the Microsoft Foundry portal?

options.why: Correct. The agent runs on a model deployment in the project.

options.text: Instructions that define the agent's behavior
options.why: Correct. Instructions act as the agent's system prompt.
Network isolation is optional and is configured on the resource, not required for each agent.
Agents can run on any suitable deployed base model. Custom training is not required.
Logic Apps workflows are not part of the agent definition.

questions.explanation: A prompt agent is defined by a model deployment, instructions and optional tools.

questions.question: You need an agent to calculate totals from a CSV file that a user uploads and to return a chart. Which tool should you add?

options.why: Azure AI Search retrieves content from an index. It does not run calculations or draw charts.
Correct. Code interpreter writes and runs Python in a sandbox, which suits calculations and charts.
File search retrieves text passages. It does not perform calculations on tabular data.
Web search retrieves public information and does not process uploaded files.

questions.explanation: Code interpreter lets an agent run Python code to analyze data and create files such as charts.

questions.question: You modify the instructions of an existing agent in the Microsoft Foundry portal and save the change. What happens?

options.text: The existing agent definition is overwritten and the previous instructions are lost.
options.why: Previous versions are kept. Each version is immutable.

options.text: A new version of the agent is created.
options.why: Correct. Each create or update produces a new, immutable agent version.

options.text: The model deployment is redeployed with the new instructions.
options.why: Instructions belong to the agent, not to the model deployment.

options.text: A new Foundry project is created for the agent.
options.why: Saving an agent does not create a project.

questions.explanation: Agents are versioned. Saving changes creates a new immutable version, so earlier versions remain available.

questions.question: You want to test how an agent responds to questions and which tools it calls before any client application code is written. What should you use?

options.text: The agent playground in the Microsoft Foundry portal
options.why: Correct. The agent playground lets you chat with the agent and inspect tool calls without code.
Metrics show usage and performance, not an interactive test chat.
The pricing calculator estimates cost and cannot run an agent.

options.text: Azure Cloud Shell with the Azure CLI only
options.why: The CLI manages resources but is not the interactive testing surface for agents.

questions.explanation: The agent playground is the no-code test surface for agents in the Foundry portal.
